title: International Relations
summary: Learn how the world works: actors and sovereignty, major IR theories, the UN, AU and regional bodies, conflict and peacekeeping, international law and human rights, global political economy and diplomacy, from African perspectives.
audience: Students, aspiring diplomats, journalists, NGO staff and engaged citizens

body.p: International relations (IR) studies how states and other actors interact across borders: war and peace, trade and money, diplomacy, international law, human rights, migration, climate change and global health.

list: States: the main actors, sovereign within their borders.
Intergovernmental organisations (IGOs): the United Nations, African Union, regional economic communities, World Bank and IMF.
Non-governmental organisations (NGOs): humanitarian groups, human-rights organisations and advocacy networks.
Multinational corporations with global economic power.
Non-state armed groups, diasporas, cities and influential individuals.

body.p: The modern state system is often traced to the Peace of Westphalia (1648), which established principles of sovereignty and non-interference. Most African states gained sovereignty in the decolonisation wave of the 1950s to 1970s. The tension between sovereignty and international concern for human rights runs through modern IR.

body.tip: When reading world news, identify the actors involved and their interests before judging the event.

body.p: Theories offer different lenses for explaining world politics. Each highlights some features and neglects others.

list: Realism: states act in their own interest in an anarchic system with no world government; power, especially military power, matters most, and conflict is a constant risk.
Liberalism: cooperation is possible and beneficial through trade, democracy, international institutions and law.
Constructivism: identities, ideas and norms shape how states define their interests; for example, norms against colonialism changed what states considered acceptable.
Marxist and dependency theories: global capitalism creates unequal relations between wealthy core states and poorer peripheral states, a view influential in analysing Africa's position.
Postcolonial and feminist perspectives: highlight how colonial histories, race and gender shape global power and whose voices are heard.

body.p: Analysts often combine theories: realism may explain an arms race while liberalism explains trade agreements between the same countries.

body.tip: Apply two theories to the same event and compare their explanations; it sharpens your analysis.

body.p: The UN, founded in 1945, has 193 member states. The General Assembly gives every state one vote. The Security Council has 15 members: 5 permanent members with veto power (China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States) and 10 elected members serving two-year terms, of which three seats are allocated to African states. Africa has long called for permanent representation on the Council. UN agencies include WHO, UNICEF, UNHCR and the World Food Programme.

list: The African Union (AU), founded in 2002 as successor to the Organisation of African Unity (1963), has 55 member states and works on peace and security, integration and governance; Agenda 2063 sets its long-term vision.

Regional economic communities include ECOWAS (West Africa), the EAC (East Africa), SADC (Southern Africa) and COMESA. ECOWAS had 15 members until Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger withdrew, taking effect in 2025, leaving 12.
The African Continental Free Trade Area aims to create a continent-wide single market.

body.tip: Check which regional organisations your country belongs to; many people belong to several overlapping ones.

body.p: Most wars today are within states rather than between them, often involving disputes over power, identity, resources and governance, sometimes with outside involvement.

list: Diplomacy and mediation by states, regional bodies and respected individuals.
Peacekeeping: UN and AU missions monitor ceasefires and protect civilians; many of the world's peacekeepers come from African countries.
Sanctions: economic or political penalties to change behaviour.
Peacebuilding: rebuilding institutions, disarming and reintegrating fighters, and reconciliation, as in post-conflict truth commissions.

body.p: Security now includes terrorism and violent extremism, piracy, cyber threats, organised crime, pandemics and the effects of climate change on resources and migration. "Human security" puts people's safety from violence, hunger and disease, not only state borders, at the centre of security policy.

body.tip: Look for root causes such as exclusion, inequality or resource disputes; lasting peace usually depends on addressing them.

body.p: International law consists of treaties, customary practices and general principles that govern relations between states and, increasingly, the rights and duties of individuals.

list: The International Court of Justice (ICJ) settles disputes between states.

The International Criminal Court (ICC) prosecutes individuals for genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity; its relationship with African states has been debated, with criticism that it has focused heavily on African cases.
International humanitarian law (the Geneva Conventions) protects civilians and prisoners in war.
Human-rights treaties, including the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights, enforced partly through the African Commission and the African Court on Human and Peoples' Rights.
The Responsibility to Protect (R2P) holds that the international community may act when a state fails to protect its population from mass atrocities.

body.p: Enforcement is a central challenge: there is no world police, so compliance relies on reputation, reciprocity, domestic courts, sanctions and political pressure.

body.tip: When assessing a claim of a law breach, ask which treaty or rule applies, who is bound by it and who can enforce it.

list: Trade rules are set through the World Trade Organization and regional and bilateral agreements.
The IMF supports countries facing balance-of-payments crises, often with policy conditions; the World Bank finances development.
Debt: many African countries face high debt-service costs, prompting calls for reform of global finance.
New partners, such as China, the Gulf states, India and Turkey, have expanded Africa's options for trade, investment and infrastructure finance.
Climate finance: debates over funding for adaptation and loss and damage for vulnerable countries.

body.p: Diplomacy is the conduct of relations through negotiation, embassies, summits and multilateral forums. Foreign policy is shaped by national interests, leaders, domestic politics, identity and geography. Soft power, the ability to attract through culture, values and policies, complements hard power. African countries increasingly pursue collective positions, for example in climate negotiations and on reforming global institutions.

body.tip: Read your foreign ministry's statements on a current issue and identify the interests and values they express.

quiz.q: The Peace of Westphalia (1648) is associated with:
Which theory stresses power and self-interest in an anarchic system?
Which theory emphasises ideas, identities and norms?
How many member states does the UN have?
How many permanent members of the Security Council have a veto?
How many elected (non-permanent) seats does the Security Council have?
How many member states does the African Union have?
After three Sahel states withdrew in 2025, ECOWAS has how many members?

options: People's safety from violence, hunger and disease

quiz.q: Which court settles disputes between states?
The Geneva Conventions are part of:
Which institution supports countries in balance-of-payments crises?

options: Attraction through culture, values and policies
